newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada approves injectable birth control method.
newsitem.headline: Canada approves injectable birth control method.

text.p: Canada's health ministry has finally approved the controversial Depo-Provera for birth control use in Canada.

Depo-Provera, or medroxyprogesterone acetate is an injection required every three months. The birth control method is more than 99 percent effective and costs about the same as the birth control pill, the producers of the drug, Pharmacia & Upjohn Inc, said in a statement on Tuesday.
"It's a serious option for a certain category of people," Dr. Andre Lalonde, executive vice-president of the Society of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, said in a phone interview in Ottawa.
But the approval has taken years. Health Canada rejected the drug in the early 1990s because officials were concerned about an increased risk of breast cancer, Lalonde said.
Canadians were also upset about reports the drug was being used on aboriginal and poor women without their consent, he added.
But new research has dissipated the concerns of Canada's scientific community, Lalonde said. More than 100 countries have approved Depo Provera.
Pharmacia & Upjohn appealed Health Canada's earlier rejection of the drug, and a Heath Canada official confirmed on Tuesday that the department had approved its use as a contraceptive.

The official said an appeals committee recommended the drug, saying the risk of women under 35 developing breast cancer from use of the drug was "very small or implausible" and rose only slightly for women over 35.

Women should inform themselves about the side effects of Depo Provera before they use it, Lalonde said. Women may have irregular bleeding or stop menstruating altogether while the drug is active and for up to nine months afterwards, but fertility should be back to normal within two years, he said.
